name: Bernard Arnault
title: The Man Who Bought a Name
subtitle: A construction heir from industrial northern France, and a pianist who knew he was not good enough, builds the world's largest luxury group around one name.
hook: In ==1971==, a 22-year-old French engineering graduate got talking to a New York taxi driver who said he loved France. Could he name the French president? "I'm afraid not, but I know Christian Dior." Thirteen years later, that passenger's family put up ==$15 million== towards a bankrupt textile group that also made disposable nappies. __He wanted it mainly for one thing: the Dior name.__ That deal became the cornerstone of LVMH, the largest luxury group on Earth.

glance.label: Grew up
glance.value: In Roubaix, where his father ran a family construction firm. He trained as a classical pianist, then judged he was not good enough to turn professional.

glance.label: Education
glance.value: The Roubaix lycée, then Lycée Faidherbe in Lille, then the elite École Polytechnique, graduating in 1971

glance.label: First job
glance.value: Engineer at Ferret-Savinel, the family construction company, from 1971

glance.label: First company (age)
glance.value: No garage start-up. He became chairman of the family firm at 29, in 1978, then at 35 bought into luxury through the 1984 Boussac and Dior deal.

glance.label: Main company today
glance.value: LVMH: chairman and CEO since 1989. It has more than 75 Maisons, over 211,000 employees and €80.8 billion of 2025 revenue. Shareholders have raised the age limit for his jobs to 85.

glance.label: Source of wealth
glance.value: LVMH. Forbes put him and his family at $117.4 billion, #17 in the world, on 1 November 2026. This number moves daily with the share price.

glance.label: Family
glance.value: Married to concert pianist Hélène Mercier. Five adult children, all in executive roles at LVMH.

glance.label: Known for
glance.value: Building the world's largest luxury group from Dior. Also for the nickname "The Terminator", earned when about 9,000 Boussac jobs were cut.

contact.howToReach: We found no public email or phone line for Mr Arnault himself, so aim for the door built for your purpose instead of the switchboard. Founders should apply to La Maison des Startups LVMH through its VivaTech application page (the last round closed on 30 April 2026, so check for the next one), young fashion designers to the LVMH Prize, and students to the LVMH careers and graduate programmes. His personal X account only opened in July 2026 and we found no evidence that he answers strangers there, so treat a reply as a public note, not a way in. Never turn up at an office or store, or buy a "contact list": it will not work and it burns your name. Keep your message to five lines: who you are, what you built, one number that proves it, which Maison it helps, and the exact thing you want.

factCheck.method: Identity and career basics were checked against LVMH's own biography and cross-read with Forbes, Britannica, Time and Bloomberg. The taxi story is taken from Arnault's own words in his 2016 Oxford Union Q&A and a 2017 WWD interview. Every contact channel was read on the organisation's own page; every social handle on LVMH's site, on the LinkedIn page itself, or in Business of Fashion/Bloomberg and Spear's reporting. Photo licences came from the Wikimedia Commons API. Apart from LinkedIn, the social profile pages could not be opened by automated tools, so those handles rest on the cited pages, not on the profiles themselves. For the same reason, official Louis Vuitton and Dior accounts were left out rather than cited to third-party directories. Mobile numbers of outside PR consultants, and an individual staff email in the Fondation's legal notice, were published but deliberately left out.

disputed.claim: The taxi ride took place in 1971, on his first trip to New York.
disputed.note: Arnault himself dates it to 1971 in the Oxford Union Q&A and in WWD (2017), and Forbes (2019) agrees. Bloomberg (2024) says 'early '70s'. Fortune (2023) places it on a later trip to grow the family business in the US. We use his own date. He also told WWD it happened 'while I studied in the U.S.', while at Oxford he described arriving at Kennedy airport for the first time. Treat it as his own recollection: we found no independent record.

He tells it slightly differently each time. WWD 2017: 'I'm afraid not, but I know Christian Dior.' WWD 2007 and Forbes 2019: 'No, but I know Christian Dior.' Oxford 2016: 'No, I don't know the French president. But I know Christian Dior.' The hook quotes the WWD 2017 version verbatim.

disputed.claim: Thirteen years passed between the taxi ride and the Dior deal.
disputed.note: 1971 to 1984 is 13 years by date arithmetic. In WWD 2017 Arnault says 'Fifteen years went by', a loose figure in speech. We use 13.

disputed.claim: What he paid for Boussac and Dior in 1984.
disputed.note: Britannica and the International Directory of Business Biographies give about $80 million in total, with $15 million from the Arnault family and the rest arranged through Lazard. Other reports describe a symbolic one-franc price, and Fortune (2023) openly notes that accounts differ. The sums may describe different parts of the deal. We state only the $15 million family stake, which Forbes also confirms, and do not state the one-franc figure as fact.

disputed.claim: When he took charge of the family firm.
disputed.note: LVMH's own biography says he became chairman in 1978, at 29. Britannica says he took control in 1971, and Forbes (2019) says he took charge at 25. We use LVMH's date.

disputed.claim: How he won control of LVMH in 1989.
disputed.note: LVMH's biography says he became majority shareholder in 1989. The International Directory of Business Biographies describes an initial 24 percent stake and a bitter fight, with Henry Racamier ousted after more than a year; Britannica dates that to 1990. The 'since 1989' in the glance follows LVMH. The companies chapter should tell the full fight.
Bloomberg (2024) calls her a pharmacist. Investopedia and other profiles stress her love of Dior and her wish that he learn piano. Left out of the glance because it could not be settled here.

The figure depends on source and date. The Forbes real-time page showed $117.4 billion on 1 November 2026, while the Observer cited $147 billion for the family in August 2026. Always show it with its date, or replace it with a fresh figure before publishing.

disputed.claim: The Fondation Louis Vuitton's visitor email domain.
disputed.note: The Fondation's contact and visit pages give contact@fondationlouisvuitton.com, while its legal notice gives the same address at .fr. We list the .com version, shown on the page meant for visitors.
